title: Word Stress: Position, Shift and Suffix Rules

blocks.text: A prefect on assembly says, 'Please REcord your names,' and the class writes nothing, because they heard a noun. ReCORD, with the stress on the second syllable, is the verb — the instruction. REcord, stress on the first, is the thing you put on a shelf. WAEC will print both and ask which stress pattern is correct for the meaning in the sentence.

blocks.markdown:
In a word of two or more syllables, **one syllable is stressed**: it is louder, slightly longer and usually clearer in vowel quality. The others are weaker, and their vowels often reduce toward /ə/.

Paper 3 tests three skills:

- finding the stressed syllable in a given word
- shifting the stress when the same spelling is a noun in one sentence and a verb in another
- using a suffix as a clue to where the stress must fall

blocks.title: Noun first, verb second
blocks.text: For a large set of two-syllable pairs, the noun (and often the adjective) is stressed on the first syllable and the verb on the second: REcord / reCORD, CONduct / conDUCT, OBject / obJECT, PREsent / preSENT, IMport / imPORT, PERmit / perMIT, CONflict / conFLICT, INcrease / inCREASE. Learn the pattern; do not memorise only one pair.

rows: REcord — a disc, a file, a past result
reCORD — to write or tape something down
conDUCT — to lead or carry out
PREsent — a gift; also the adjective 'current'
blocks.caption: Stress shift that changes word class

items: **Suffixes -tion and -sion** pull the stress onto the syllable immediately before them: *educAtion*, *inforMAtion*, *deciSION*, *occaSION*.
**Compound nouns** usually stress the first element: *BLACKboard*, *GREENhouse*, *FOOTball*, *CLASSroom*.
**PHOtograph → phoTOgraphy → photoGRAPHic** shows stress moving as suffixes are added; never assume the stress of the root survives.

blocks.title: Predicting stress from a suffix
blocks.prompt: Where does the stress fall in education, and how do you know without looking it up?

steps.text: Spot the suffix. Education ends in -tion, one of the suffixes that pull stress onto the syllable just before them.
Count back one syllable from -tion: e-du-CA-tion. The stressed syllable is CA.
Check a second -tion word by the same rule: in-for-MA-tion. The rule holds.
Contrast with the verb educate, which is EDucate — first-syllable stress. Adding -tion has moved the stress.
Apply the same logic to decision (de-CI-sion) and to the compound noun blackboard (BLACK-board, first element).

blocks.answer: educAtion — stress on the syllable immediately before -tion.

blocks.title: WAEC Oral English tip
blocks.text: When the options print a word with one syllable in capital letters (CONduct, conDUCT), read the sentence first and decide whether you need a noun or a verb. Then pick the pattern that matches: first syllable for the noun, second for the verb. For -tion/-sion items, ignore the root you think you know and stress the syllable before the suffix.

points: Every polysyllabic word has one main stress; the other syllables are weaker.
Many noun–verb pairs shift: REcord (noun) versus reCORD (verb).
Suffixes -tion, -sion, -ic and -ity pull stress onto the syllable before them.
Compound nouns such as blackboard and football stress the first element.
Adding a suffix can move the stress, as in photograph / photography / photographic.
